question.text: A working transistor with its three legs marked <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi></math>, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="normal">Q</mi></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi></math> is tested using a multimeter. No conduction is found between <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="normal">Q</mi></math>. By connecting the common (negative) terminal of the multimeter to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi></math> and the other (positive) terminal to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="normal">Q</mi></math>, some resistance is seen on the multimeter. Which of the following is true for the transistor?

options.text: It is an n-p-n transistor with R as base
It is an p-n-p transistor with R as collector
It is an p-n-p transistor with R as emitter
It is an n-p-n transistor with R as collector

solution.text: Since no conduction is found when the multimeter is connected across P and Q it means either both P and Q are n-type or p-type. So, it means R is base. When R is connected to the common terminal and conduction is seen when another terminal is connected to P and Q, so it means transistor is in n-p-n configuration with R as the base.
